deep.reconstruction:
This page contains no mathematics. It is a continuous German prose text on ancient history. It reads like lecture or school notes on the Persian Empire, continuing from folio 43 (Thermopylae, Salamis, Plataea, Mycale). In paraphrase:

- The Greeks became masters of the sea, which weakened the interior of the Persian realm, and the way to Asia stood open to them.
- In 465 Xerxes was murdered by Artabanus and an accomplice (the name is unclear in the hand).
- His son Artaxerxes Longimanus succeeded him only after bloodshed, because he refused to recognise his elder brother.
- The Greeks, led by Cimon, an arch-enemy of the Persians, threatened Cyprus with a fleet. The Persians, close to losing it, sought peace.
- In 449 a peace glorious for Greece was concluded (the so-called Peace of Callias). Its terms:
  - Persia gives up all claims on the Asiatic Greeks.
  - Persia keeps its fleets within a fixed boundary and does not appear in the Aegean.
  - Persian land armies stay 30 miles from the coast.

There are no formulas, computations, figures or marginal mathematical notes on the page. The right-hand strip visible in the image is the edge of the facing folio (the next page's text). The handwriting and content suggest notes copied from a history course, possibly not by Gauss himself. Nothing mathematical is present to reconstruct.
errors: Historical remark: the 'Peace of Callias' of 449 BC is traditionally dated after Cimon's death (450/449) during the Cyprus campaign. Its historicity is debated. The 30-mile clause is usually given in ancient sources as a day's ride or three days' march; the figure is a stock textbook formulation.
Xerxes' murder in 465 is usually attributed to Artabanus, with the eunuch Aspamitres (Mithridates) as accomplice. The transcribed name 'Seguinten' is likely a mis-reading or garbled name.

results.what: Narrative summary of Persian–Greek history 465–449 BC (death of Xerxes, accession of Artaxerxes I, Cimon at Cyprus, Peace of Callias)
results.modern_name: Standard ancient-history textbook content (Peace of Callias)

deep.surprise_reason: The page is non-mathematical history notes (Persian Wars), routine textbook content with no scientific significance.
transcription_corrections: Page number at top left reads '44', not '47[?]', consistent with folio 44.
'Am mächtigsten[?] waren jetzt die Kriege[?]' more plausibly reads 'Am nachtheiligsten wurden jetzt die Kriege der Griechen', i.e. most damaging to Persia, which fits the context.
'Cimon' is underlined in the manuscript (as is 'Cyprus').
'von Seguinten[?]' is uncertain; historically one expects a name such as Mithridates/Aspamitres alongside Artabanus.
The marginal fragments on the right ('Artaxerxes', 'bis 404', 'Darius' ...) belong to the facing next page, not to this folio.
